---
title: "Bayes at the Edge"
abstract: |
  Accuracy-first epistemology defends Bayesian conditionalization by showing that, among rules that respond only to what one learns, it does best by the lights of accuracy. Externalists who think inexact knowledge needs a margin for error face a problem: such agents can learn something without learning that it is what they learned, and then other rules do better. Meehan and Zhang argue that conditionalization can be restored. Among rules whose output depends only on the prior and on what is learned, it has the highest expected accuracy summed over every possible way of learning. I argue that the restoration fails for the agents who motivate it. If every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude leaves a margin for error around the truth, then the truth is never at the edge of what she learns, and conditionalization is accuracy-dominated by a rule that responds only to what she learns. Meehan and Zhang's sum avoids this result by counting, with equal weight, learning in which the truth does sit at the edge; statisticians call this condition coarsening at random, and margins forbid it. What accuracy recommends instead is certainty that is not knowledge. So accuracy-first epistemology and knowledge-first externalism cannot share conditionalization.
bibliography: bayes-at-the-edge.bib
---

# The problem {#sec-intro}

Bayesian conditionalization says that when one learns *p*, and nothing stronger, one should adopt one's prior conditional on *p*. Its best-known defence is accuracy-theoretic. @GreavesWallace2006 showed that if the propositions one might learn form a partition, then conditionalizing has the highest expected accuracy among plans that respond only to what one learns. @BriggsPettigrew2020 turned this into a dominance argument [corrected by @Nielsen2021]. Both results presuppose that whenever one learns *p*, one is in a position to tell that *p* is what one learned.

Externalists deny this. On @Williamson2000's view, inexact knowledge requires a margin for error. Suppose the hand of an unmarked clock points at 17 and you cannot discriminate neighbouring positions. Then the most you know by looking is that it points somewhere from 16 to 18. Had it pointed at 18, you would have known only that it pointed somewhere from 17 to 19. Since 18 is compatible with what you know, you do not know that 16-to-18 is what you know. When learning is opaque in this way, the accuracy arguments turn against conditionalization. Among plans that respond only to what is learned, the one with highest expected accuracy conditionalizes on the proposition that one has learned *p*, not on *p* itself [@Schoenfield2017]. On the clock, that plan makes one certain of the hand's exact position. The externalist who wants to be a Bayesian, and to connect rationality with accuracy, seems to be stuck [@Schultheis2025].

@MeehanZhang2025 offer a way out. They require that the credence a rule recommends depend only on the prior and on the proposition learned, not on the learning situation that produced it: *global evidential constancy*. They then evaluate rules not by expected accuracy in the agent's actual situation but by *total* expected accuracy, the sum of expected accuracies over every learning situation compatible with the prior. Their main result (Fact 10, p. 330) is that among globally evidentially constant rules, conditionalization uniquely maximizes total expected accuracy. Bayes is back.

I argue that Bayes is back only for learners who lack the feature that made the problem. The central claim is a dominance result. Suppose every way an agent has of learning about a magnitude leaves a margin for error around the truth, as on Williamson's clock and in Meehan and Zhang's examples of Olivia and right-handed Dana. Then whatever she learns, the truth lies in its interior, never next to a possibility it excludes. Some globally evidentially constant rule is then at least as accurate as conditionalization at every combination of learning situation and state possible for her, and strictly more accurate whenever what she learns has an edge (@sec-dominance). Informally: knowing that you cannot tell neighbouring cases apart is information about where, within what you know, the truth lies. Conditionalization throws that information away, and pays for it at every possibility you leave open.

Meehan and Zhang's sum favours conditionalization because their measure is an instance of what statisticians call *coarsening at random*. It weights learning a proposition equally at every state where it is true, including states at its edge (@sec-edge). Margins around the truth forbid this. Their own diagnosis is that the question is "whether the (total) expected accuracy of an updating rule should be evaluated in a way that satisfies extensionality" (p. 339). For margin externalists, the answer is no. I take up their replies in @sec-whose. In @sec-recommend I ask what accuracy recommends instead, and find that it recommends certainty that is not knowledge. The conclusion (@sec-conclusion) is that accuracy-first epistemology and knowledge-first externalism cannot share conditionalization: one must give it up for inexact knowledge, or give up the claim to explain it.[^antecedents]

[^antecedents]: Several pieces have antecedents:
    - Kenny Easwaran observed, in a comment on @Pettigrew2025, that Meehan and Zhang's total amounts to expected accuracy when each learning situation is equally likely [@Easwaran2025].
    - Likelihood-weighted rules that maximize expected accuracy under uncertainty about how one learns are in @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and @EaswaranNielsen2025.
    - @Salow2018 contrasts evidence centred on the truth with evidence centred on a best guess, arguing that the former permits inquiries biased in one's favour.
    - @Dorst2020 gives a dominance argument, about credence in a single proposition, against certain clock models.

    What is new here is a dominance result that holds across every learning situation with margins around the truth and is witnessed by a globally evidentially constant rule, together with its converse; the diagnosis of how evaluations that vindicate conditionalization escape it; and the argument of @sec-recommend.

# Margins around the truth {#sec-margins}

I use Meehan and Zhang's framework.
- A *prior space* is a finite set of states *S* with a regular prior π.
- A *learning situation* is a function *E* taking each state *s* to the strongest proposition *E*(*s*) one learns there; learning is factive, so *s* ∈ *E*(*s*).
- An *updating rule* returns, for each prior space, learning situation and state, the credence to adopt there.
- A rule is *globally evidentially constant* if that credence depends only on the prior space and *E*(*s*). Equivalently (their Fact 5, p. 316), it is a function from propositions to credences, *f*(*p*). Conditionalization, *b*(*p*) = π(· | *p*), is one such rule.

Margins come from measurement. An instrument, or an eye, reports a value *a* when the true value is *v*. What can one then know? On the view @Williamson2013 offers and @Weatherson2013 defends, the strongest thing one knows after a reading *a* with error *e* = |*a* − *v*| is that the value lies within *e* + *m* of *a*, where *m* > 0 is the margin that safety requires. Every value within *m* of *v* is within *e* + *m* of *a*. So the region is centred on the appearance but always leaves a margin of *m* around the truth. Others centre what one learns on a best guess and allow no slack beyond the error [@Stalnaker2009; @CohenComesana2013; @Salow2018]. For Salow, talk of margins is talk of "the maximum distance between my best guess and the actual hand", and the truth may lie anywhere within that distance of the guess, edge included. The argument below concerns views of the first kind. That is the kind that generates the opacity Meehan and Zhang address. Their Olivia "knows that, if the butter weighs *x* oz., then she will learn by weighing it in her hand that it weighs (*x* ± 1) oz., but nothing more precise" (p. 294), "a variant of the austere clock from Williamson" (p. 294, n. 6).

To fit this into the framework, take the states to be values of a magnitude, ordered on a line or round a circle, at increments no larger than the margin. Two states are *neighbours* if they are adjacent. Williamson's margin principle, with what one learns identified with what one comes to know (which Meehan and Zhang cite as "one influential externalist view of evidence", p. 290, n. 4), says that the strongest proposition learned at *s* contains *s*'s neighbours. Call a learning situation *two-sided* if, for every *s*, *E*(*s*) contains *s* and its neighbours. Margins may be wider than one step and may vary from state to state; only the immediate neighbours matter here. For a proposition *p*, let its *interior* be the set of states of *p* whose neighbours all lie in *p*, and its *rim* the rest of *p*: the states sitting next to a state that *p* excludes.

**Observation.** If *E* is two-sided and *E*(*s*) = *p*, then *s* is in the interior of *p*.

If *s* were on the rim, one of its neighbours would lie outside *p*. But a two-sided *E*(*s*) contains all of *s*'s neighbours. @Williamson2014 [p. 980] proves the special case for his clock, where what is known at *w* is the interval of width 2*h* + 1 centred on *w*: "R(w) is known only at w". So Olivia learns that the butter weighs from 16 to 18 oz. only if it weighs 17. Dana weighs butter of 15, 16 or 17 oz. with her right hand, and her prior is (0.2, 0.6, 0.2) (pp. 300–301). She learns {15, 16} only at 15. One caveat: the margin must have positive width relative to the prior. If the grid is refined while the margin stays one step wide, the rim's probability, and with it everything below, shrinks to zero. Williamson's margins are fixed in physical units, so refining the grid widens them in steps.

# Conditionalization is dominated {#sec-dominance}

An accuracy measure assigns a score *A*(*c*, *s*) to credence function *c* at state *s*. The logarithmic score is ln *c*(*s*). The Brier score is minus the sum, over propositions, of the squared distance between one's credence in a proposition and its truth value. Meehan and Zhang use this and an additive logarithmic score of the same propositionwise form (p. 302). Both are additive, continuous and strictly proper in the sense of @Predd2009.

**Proposition.** Let *A* be the logarithmic score, or any additive, continuous, strictly proper score, and let π be regular. There is a globally evidentially constant rule *f*~*A*~ such that, for every two-sided learning situation *E* and every state *s*,

> *A*(*f*~*A*~(*E*(*s*)), *s*) ≥ *A*(π(· | *E*(*s*)), *s*),

with strict inequality whenever *E*(*s*) has a nonempty rim. On a connected scale, that is whenever anything short of the whole space is learned. Conversely, a globally evidentially constant rule is undominated across two-sided learning iff it concentrates its credence on the interior of every proposition with a nonempty interior.

*Proof.* Let *p* have a nonempty interior and a nonempty rim, and let *c* = π(· | *p*). By the Observation, a two-sided learner who learns *p* is at an interior state. So it suffices to compare credences at interior states.

*Logarithmic score.* Let *f*~*A*~(*p*) = π(· | int *p*). For interior *s*, π(*s* | int *p*) = π(*s*)/π(int *p*) > π(*s*)/π(*p*) = π(*s* | *p*), because regularity gives the rim positive probability.

*Additive scores.* Treat a credence function over *S* as a forecast for the events *X* ∩ int *p*, for *X* ⊆ *S*, with the interior of *p* as the space of possibilities. At an interior state, *X* ∩ int *p* is true iff *X* is. So the forecast's penalty there, in Predd et al.'s sense, is just its score. Since *c* gives the rim positive probability, no probability measure on the interior agrees with it: it is incoherent relative to that space. By Predd et al.'s Theorem 1(b), which covers bounded and unbounded scores, *c* is strongly dominated at every interior state by a coherent forecast, that is, by a credence function concentrated on the interior. Let *f*~*A*~(*p*) be one. For the Brier score it is the Euclidean projection of *c*, which adds the rim's probability equally to each interior state.

For every other proposition, let *f*~*A*~(*p*) = *c*. A two-sided learner never learns a proposition with an empty interior.

*Converse.* By Predd et al.'s Theorem 1(a), a forecast coherent relative to the interior is not weakly dominated there. Every interior state is one at which some two-sided situation delivers *p*: let *E* deliver *p* there and the whole space everywhere else. ∎

Four remarks.

1. **Global evidential constancy.** The rules respond only to what is learned, so each satisfies evidential constancy and non-contrastiveness. Followability does not separate them from conditionalization. As Meehan and Zhang point out, conditionalization is no more "luminous" than its rivals in opaque problems (p. 306). Their own principle Margin (p. 305) makes rules close to a followable rule followable too. A rule that tells you to conditionalize on what you learned asks no less of your capacity to tell what you learned than one that tells you to discount its rim.

2. **Dependence on the score.** The dominating rule depends on the score, as Joyce's dominating credences do [@Joyce1998]. With two or more interior states, no single rule dominates conditionalization under every score. That conditionalization is dominated does not depend on the score.

3. **Examples.**
   - Suppose Olivia's prior is uniform. When the butter weighs 17 she learns [16, 18], and conditionalization gives each weight credence 1/3. The dominating rules make her certain of 17, and she is right, since [16, 18] is learned only at 17.
   - At 15, Dana's conditionalized credence (0.25, 0.75, 0) has Brier score −2.25. That is worse even than the −2.08 of keeping her prior (p. 302, Table 1). The dominating rule scores 0.

4. **Uniformity.** Meehan and Zhang show that for every globally evidentially constant rule, some problem favours another: "There is no rule that rules them all" (p. 327). Their Fact 7 (p. 324) says no such rule does at least as well as conditionalization in every problem. Its proof uses, for each *p*, the transparent problem of learning whether *p*. There *p* is learned at every state where it is true, rim included. Restrict attention to two-sided problems and the situation reverses: a single rule does at least as well as conditionalization in all of them.

So conditionalization is suboptimal under every weighting of two-sided learning situations that gives weight to learning some proposition with a rim, whatever the weights mean.

The result inverts @BriggsPettigrew2020: for partitional learning every rule but conditionalization is dominated; for two-sided learning, conditionalization is. It differs from @Dorst2020, whose dominance argument concerns credence in a single proposition, and from @Schoenfield2017, whose meta-conditionalization responds to the learning situation, not just to what is learned.

## Graded margins

Real discrimination is graded. Psychometric functions slope, and "cannot tell apart" is a threshold set at some performance level. If learning is stochastic, the truth occasionally falls on the rim of what is learned, and pointwise dominance fails. A rule certain of the interior is infinitely wrong under the log score in those rare cases.

What remains is a comparison of expected accuracy. By Meehan and Zhang's Lemma 1 (p. 344), the globally evidentially constant rule with highest expected accuracy gives each state of *p* credence proportional to π(*s*)λ~*p*~(*s*), where λ~*p*~(*s*) is the probability of learning *p* at *s*. Conditionalization is optimal only if λ~*p*~ is flat across *p*. When the probability of learning *p* falls off toward its edge, the optimal rule raises the centre and lowers the rim, as in the "cosine" dial of @EaswaranNielsen2025 [p. 1129]. The graded case changes the verdict from dominance to expected inferiority. It does not change its direction.

# How Bayes comes back {#sec-edge}

Why, then, does Meehan and Zhang's total favour conditionalization? Let λ weight learning situations, and let λ~*p*~(*s*) be the total weight of situations in which *p* is learned at *s*. Read λ as a probability of being in each situation. Then their Lemma 1 says that the best rule conditionalizes on the fact that *p* was learned, with λ~*p*~(*s*) as the likelihood. This is Easwaran's observation: the total is "basically equivalent to assuming you are equally likely to be using it in any of these situations" [@Easwaran2025]. Conditionalization on *p* itself is best iff λ~*p*~(*s*) is the same at every state of *p*. This is Meehan and Zhang's *extensionality* (Fact 11, p. 337; Lemma 2, p. 345).

Statisticians call this condition *coarsening at random*: data are coarsened at random when the probability of observing a set is the same at every point of the set [@HeitjanRubin1991]. @Gill1997 showed that, under this condition and only under it, conditioning on the observed set agrees with conditioning on the fact that it was observed; @GrunwaldHalpern2003 [Theorem 3.1] restate the result for updating. As @GillGrunwald2008 [p. 2410] put it, the condition "precisely characterizes when one can ignore the distinction between the fact that an event has been observed, and the fact that an event has happened". Monty Hall is the standard illustration. Meehan and Zhang mention it in discussing Pearl's lesson that "we must also consider what information could have been reported" (p. 311, n. 21). Their extensionality is coarsening at random, and Fact 11 is an instance of the statistical characterization.

Their own measure weights every factive learning situation equally, so it is coarsened at random. In Easwaran's gloss, which proposition one learns is "chosen uniformly at random from the set of all propositions true at the world" [@Easwaran2025]. So the total credits each proposition as if it were learned equally often at each of its states, rim included.[^perm]

[^perm]: Any weighting unchanged by permutations of the states is extensional. If *s* and *s*′ both lie in *p*, the transposition of *s* and *s*′ maps the situations delivering *p* at *s* one-to-one onto those delivering *p* at *s*′, preserving weight. The counting measure is permutation-invariant because it treats *S* as an unstructured set. Margins are defined by adjacency, and a weighting that respects adjacency need not be permutation-invariant.

For a two-sided learner, extensionality is not merely contestable but impossible. The argument has three steps:
1. Extensionality requires the weight on learning *p* to be the same at every state of *p*.
2. By the Observation, two-sided situations deliver *p* only at its interior, so a weighting confined to them puts no weight on learning *p* at its rim.
3. Such a weighting is therefore extensional only if no proposition with a rim gets positive weight. On a connected scale, that means nothing is learned but the whole space.

In the statistical idiom: margins around the truth guarantee that coarsening is not at random.

Coarsening at random can be restored with mixtures, but only by adding learning that is exact at an edge. On Dana's scale, mix her right-hand situation with gauges that err in one direction only, weighted as follows. The columns give what is learned at 15, 16 and 17.

| Weight | At 15 | At 16 | At 17 | |
|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---:|:---|
| 2/7 | {15} | *S* | *S* | |
| 1/7 | {15, 16} | *S* | {16, 17} | Dana's right hand |
| 1/7 | *S* | {15, 16} | {16, 17} | |
| 1/7 | *S* | *S* | {17} | |
| 2/7 | *S* | {16, 17} | *S* | |

Now {15, 16} has weight 1/7 at each of its states, {16, 17} has 2/7 at each, and *S* has 4/7 at each. The mixture is coarsened at random, and conditionalization is again optimal. The work is done by situations that deliver {15, 16} or {16, 17} at 16. These are gauges with no margin on the side facing the excluded value, which a two-sided learner never uses. Even then the proportions must be exactly right. @GrunwaldHalpern2003 [§4] show that, for overlapping observations, coarsening at random holds only in special cases.

The same pattern runs through models in which conditionalization has seemed accuracy-friendly despite opacity:
- @Carr2021's clock spreads prior credence evenly over world–evidence pairs.
- Isaacs and Russell's clock lets the guess fall equally often one step either side of the truth.
- Easwaran and Nielsen's uniform-error clock is conditionalization-friendly because "for every signal, every world that gives it a non-zero probability gives it the same probability" [@EaswaranNielsen2025, p. 1120; cf. @IsaacsRussell2023, Theorem 4].

In each, the truth is as likely to be at the edge of what is conditioned on as in its middle. This requires, though it is not secured by, the absence of slack: Easwaran and Nielsen's clock with likelihoods 1/4, 1/2, 1/4 has no slack and is still not coarsened at random. Coarsening at random also suffices for the other attractions of conditionalization. The expected posterior then equals the prior, and expected accuracy is at least that of not updating [@Good1967]. So the predictable biases of conditionalizing on opaque evidence that @Salow2018, @AhmedSalow2019 and @Das2023 describe all require that it fail, though they do not follow from its failure.

# Whose accuracy? {#sec-whose}

Meehan and Zhang anticipate the obvious complaint: "By stipulation, Dana knows her learning situation", and other rules do better in it, so why should she care how conditionalization fares elsewhere (p. 333)? They distinguish two versions.

The first holds that "the rational updating rule just is the rule that recommends the most accurate updating plan in every updating problem" (p. 334). They reply that this rejects global evidential constancy, and with it conditionalization, so it is the "radical response" of @Gallow2021, @IsaacsRussell2023 and others. Their aim is to show it is "not the only option" (p. 334). The second version questions the equal weighting, and leads to extensionality, the point they call "close to the bedrock of normative explanations" (p. 337).

The Proposition changes the first version. The complaint is no longer that different problems call for different plans. It is that for an agent who knows her learning is two-sided, a single globally evidentially constant rule beats conditionalization in every problem she could be in. What remains of the dispute is whether one rule must serve agents who know different things about how they learn.

Here I own the contrast. Right-handed Dana should adopt a rule that left-handed Dana should not. Her left hand "can tell … whether or not it weighs 17 oz." (p. 320), so her learning with it is partitional, and Greaves and Wallace's argument applies. So the view defended here is contrastive in Meehan and Zhang's sense. By their Fact 6 (p. 320), it therefore violates their formal idempotence condition. Their own sequence shows the cost. Suppose Dana weighs with her right hand and then with her left, and her credence is a function of the conjunction of what she has learned. Then she goes from certainty that the butter weighs 15 to one-quarter confidence on learning {15, 16} a second time. That is the charge they press against meta-conditionalization (pp. 320–321, n. 30).

But consider what drives it. Her credence depends on which hand delivered {15, 16}, not just on the proposition {15, 16}. The formal condition demands the opposite: credence must be a function of the conjunction of what has been learned, whatever the route. That is coarsening at random once more, in normative dress. Meehan and Zhang's slogan, "same prior over *S*, same evidence about *S*, same posterior over *S*" (p. 309), says what could have been learned instead is "neither here nor there" (p. 319). Monty Hall is the standard counterexample. They reconcile it with non-contrastiveness by refining the state space so that Monty's protocol is part of what is learned (p. 311, n. 21). They grant that in opaque versions, where that refinement is unavailable, "it is less obvious that the standard solution still applies". The present cases are opaque Monty Halls.

The intuition that learning the same thing again should change nothing is respected if Dana's credence responds to what each hand delivered. It fails only if her credence must respond to the conjunction alone. Meehan and Zhang hold that Dana cannot use her knowledge of her right hand's structure, because although she learns {15, 16}, "she does not learn that that is what she learns" (p. 321, n. 29). The Proposition shows she does not need to learn it. A rule that responds only to {15, 16} does the work.

The second version leads to the strongest reply available to Meehan and Zhang. Total expected accuracy is meant to be "part of an objective measure of how accurate the updating rule is in general for any agent, irrespective of their uncertainties about their evidential situations" (p. 330, n. 35). Read this way, extensionality is the evaluative counterpart of global evidential constancy. If a rule's output may depend only on the prior and *p*, its grade may depend only on how the prior, given *p*, expects that output to fare. That is exactly what the counting measure computes, since for globally evidentially constant rules the total is a weighted sum, over propositions *p*, of the accuracy π(· | *p*) expects of the rule's response to *p* (their proof of Fact 10, pp. 332–333).

This defence works, but consider what it vindicates. Conditionalization is then the best support function: the best way of scoring hypotheses against a proposition, for an assessor who abstracts from how the proposition was learned. That is a vindication of evidential probability as a measure. It is not a vindication of the choice that any agent who knows her margins should make. Right-handed Dana can see that the rule so vindicated is dominated for her by another that satisfies every constraint Meehan and Zhang impose.

Pettigrew puts the point in his gloss on the result: "the negative expected effects of being exposed to certain evidence functions and conditionalizing on them are counterbalanced by the positive expected effects of doing this when exposed to other evidence functions". He adds that it "relies on you thinking each evidence function is equally likely" [@Pettigrew2025]. For the two-sided learner, the counterbalancing is done by learners at the edge.

Two smaller points. First, an agent who is certain only that her learning is two-sided, with margins of unknown and varying width, is still covered by the Proposition, which assumes nothing more. If she gives some credence to learning that is exact at an edge, the comparison is one of expected accuracy. Conditionalization is then optimal only if her credences happen to be coarsened at random. Credences tied to the actual structure of how she learns have no reason to be.

Second, Meehan and Zhang suggest Bayesianism may be a theory of "high-level" rationality that abstracts from "individual psychological dispositions and environmental conditions" (p. 338). If so, the Proposition says which abstraction the high level requires: from whether one's knowledge has margins around the truth. That is the feature the problem began with (p. 294).

# What accuracy recommends {#sec-recommend}

If conditionalization is dominated, what does accuracy recommend? By the converse in @sec-dominance, the undominated globally evidentially constant rules for two-sided learning are those that give the rim no credence at all. Rules that give the rim some credence are dominated by their projections. For an agent who knows exactly how she learns, the verdict is starker. Olivia learns each proposition at only one state, so her only undominated response is certainty of that state, which is Schoenfield's meta-conditionalization as a dominance verdict.

These certainties are true but they are not knowledge. Williamson's margin principle, which generated two-sidedness in the first place, says that one knows *q* at *s* only if *q* is true at every state one cannot discriminate from *s*. Suppose Olivia, having learned [16, 18], becomes certain that the butter weighs 17. That certainty is false at 16 and at 18, which she cannot tell from 17. Conditionalization's certainties are different. The proposition [16, 18] is true throughout the margin. So there is an asymmetry. Every certainty conditionalization produces in a two-sided learner is knowledge: it is entailed by what she knows. The dominating rules produce certainty in something stronger than what she knows. Whenever she is next to the rim of what she learns, as Olivia always is, that certainty is false at a state she cannot discriminate from her own.

On Williamson's clock, being certain of the exact position *w* amounts to being certain that one knows *R*(*w*), the interval of positions within the margin of *w*. The evidential probability of that is 1/(2*h* + 1), as he shows [@Williamson2014, p. 980]. Accuracy registers none of this; safety registers all of it.

Suppose we therefore require that credence never be certain of what is not known. This is a constraint from the theory of knowledge, not from accuracy. Even so, it does not restore conditionalization. If the score is concave, as the Brier and log scores are, then for every ε between 0 and 1 the mixture (1 − ε)*f* + ε*b* scores at least (1 − ε)*A*(*f*) + ε*A*(*b*) at every state. It is therefore strictly more accurate than conditionalization wherever *f* is. Yet it is never certain of anything *b* is not certain of. This is the technique of Meehan and Zhang's Fact 4 (p. 304).

On Williamson's clock with a uniform prior, these mixtures give credences (ε/3, 1 − 2ε/3, ε/3) to the three positions one cannot rule out. With ε = 0.3, this is the credence @AhmedSalow2019 consider in their "Third Objection" (though only for the sake of argument) and the posterior that Gallow derives from probabilities of misfiring [@Gallow2021]. With ε = 3/4, it is the likelihood-weighted update of @EaswaranNielsen2025 [pp. 1120–1121]. What accuracy recommends for inexact knowers, once certainty is restricted to what is known, is what the signal theorists recommend.[^ho]

[^ho]: Higher-order principles do not favour conditionalization either. On Williamson's clock it produces Dorst's "effacing" evidence about whether the hand is at an even position [@Dorst2020]; Dorst takes this as a reason to reject such models.

So the externalist who connects rationality with accuracy faces a choice. On the clock, accuracy rewards certainty that her theory of knowledge says is not knowledge. If she blocks that with a knowledge norm, what is left of accuracy still does not favour conditionalization. What favours conditionalization is a further norm: credence should be the prior conditioned on what one knows. Accuracy plays no part in it.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

The externalist Bayesian wanted three things:
- conditionalization on what one learns;
- the opacity produced by margins around the truth;
- an explanation of conditionalization's rationality in terms of accuracy.

For inexact knowledge, the three cannot all be had.

A knowledge-first externalist can keep conditionalization on what she knows, margins and all. Rational credence is then evidential probability, the prior conditioned on one's knowledge, taken as basic [@Williamson2000; @Das2022]. This is the first of the externalist responses Meehan and Zhang describe (p. 288). The argument of @sec-recommend gives her more than a fallback. It explains why accuracy is the wrong standard here: it rewards certainty that is not knowledge. For her, the Proposition is an argument against accuracy-first epistemology's claim to explain updating.

An accuracy-first epistemologist can instead update, by prior times likelihood, on signals she responds to but need not know she has [@Gallow2021; @IsaacsRussell2023; @EaswaranNielsen2025]. She need not give up margins; Easwaran and Nielsen make no claims about how signals relate to knowledge (p. 1122). What she gives up is credence as evidential probability, and with it conditionalization on worldly propositions, except where learning is coarsened at random. A best guess that one can always identify, as in @Salow2018, is the special case in which learning becomes partitional and the original arguments apply unchanged.

Meehan and Zhang's Hi-TEA tries to have both: conditionalization on what is learned, and an accuracy vindication of it. It succeeds at the level of a support function that is impartial among ways of learning. That impartiality is coarsening at random, which is indifference to exactly the structure that makes inexact learning opaque. Their theorem is correct, and it shows something real: averaged over every way of learning, the selection effects that hurt conditionalization cancel. But they cancel because the average includes learners who can learn a proposition at its edge. For learners whose knowledge always leaves a margin around the truth, nothing cancels. Bayes is back only where the truth can sit at the edge of what one knows.
